'''Ari Brynjolfsson''' (December 7, 1926 – June 28, 2013;<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.mbl.is/greinasafn/grein/1477312/|title=Ari Brynjólfsson – Obituary|date=2013-08-24|work=[[Morgunblaðið]]}}</ref> Icelandic spelling Brynjólfsson) was an Icelandic-American nuclear physicist known for his work in America on [[food irradiation]] and for the development of radiation facilities for improving [[food safety]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Holden |first=Constance |date=1978-11-03 |title=Army Still Plugging for FDA Approval of Irradiated Meat |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.705340 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=202 |issue=4367 |pages=500–500 |doi=10.1126/science.705340 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Deitch |first=Jerome |last2=Josephson |first2=Edward F. |date=1983 |title=Economics of food irradiation |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10408398209527352 |journal=C R C Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition |language=en |volume=17 |issue=4 |pages=307–334 |doi=10.1080/10408398209527352 |issn=0099-0248|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Brynjolfsson was born in [[Akureyri, Iceland]], as one of the seven children of Brynjólfur Sigtryggsson and Guðrún Rósinkarsdóttir<ref name="Akureyri"/> from Hörgárdalur.<ref name="Timinn73"/> He lived in Krossanes, [[Eyjafjörður]]<ref name="Dagur54"/> and graduated from [[Akureyri Junior College|Menntaskólinn á Akureyri]] in 1948,<ref name="M54"/> then studied [[nuclear physics]] at the [[Niels Bohr Institute]], [[University of Copenhagen]], Denmark, from 1948 to 1954, gaining his PhD,<ref name="Obit"/> with a thesis which dealt with a device he had constructed for accurately measuring [[Rock magnetism|magnetism in rocks]].<ref name="Dagur54"/> Following this he became a special research fellow of the [[University of Iceland]] from 1954 to 1955, then an [[Alexander von Humboldt]] fellow of the [[University of Göttingen]], Germany, from 1955 to 1957.<ref name="Obit"/> While at Göttingen he contributed important work in [[magnetic moment]]s, using a self-devised instrument with which he and others provided the strongest evidence to that date for [[Geomagnetic reversal|magnetic field reversal]]s.<ref name="Glen"/>

He became Head of Radiation Facilities for the Danish government at [[Risø DTU National Laboratory for Sustainable Energy|Risø Laboratoy]] (1957–1965) and then Head of US Army Radiation Facilities, [[Natick, Massachusetts]]<ref name="Timinn73"/><ref name="Timinn65"/> (1965–1980). He graduated from the advanced management program at the [[Harvard Business School]] in 1971. He also served as the Director of IFFIT ([[International Facility for Food Irradiation Technology]]) of the Joint FAO/IAEA, [[United Nations]] (1988–1992).<ref name="CV"/> He gained his DSc in 1973 with a thesis entitled ''Some Aspects of the Interactions of Fast Charged Particles with Matter'' which led to his work on plasma redshift.<ref name="Brynjolfsson1973"/>

Later in his life, he published several articles on his results for the reverse plasma redshift of photons in a gravitational field, which led him to investigate and develop his own theory within [[Plasma cosmology]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Brynjolfsson |first1=Ari |title=Search &#124; arXiv e-print repository |url=https://arxiv.org/search/astro-ph?searchtype=author&query=Brynjolfsson%2C+A |website=arxiv |publisher=Cornell University}}</ref> In 2004 he also co-signed a letter published on [[New Scientist]] addressing the lack of funds and attention for theories alternative to [[Big Bang|Big Bang cosmology]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lerner |first1=Eric |title=Bucking the big bang |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg18224482-900-bucking-the-big-bang/ |website=New Scientist }}</ref>

Many of his publications and much of his work centered around [[food irradiation]] and the development of radiation facilities around the world.<ref name="Akureyri"/><ref name="Timinn73"/> He received several awards including the Møller Foundation Award for exceptional service to Danish Industry, 1965 "Radiation Science and Technology Award of the [[American Nuclear Society]]", 1988<ref name="OrgVa"/><ref name="Timinn88"/> and was noted award recipient from U.S. Brigadier General Merrill L. Tribe in 1963.<ref name="HI4712726"/><ref name="Timinn63"/>

He died at the age of 86 in [[Tampa, FL]] on 28 June 2013, leaving a widow, five children and nineteen grandchildren.<ref name="Obit"/>
